items.question: Trace the four Buddhist Councils, noting their venues, royal patrons and presiding monks, and explain how they shaped the Buddhist canon and the emergence of its major schools.
items.modelAnswer: The **Buddhist Councils (Sangitis)** were assemblies of monks that **codified the Buddha's teachings** and **resolved doctrinal and disciplinary disputes**. The **First Council** (c. **483 BCE**) met at **Rajagriha** under **Ajatashatru**, presided over by **Mahakassapa**; here **Upali** recited the **Vinaya Pitaka** and **Ananda** the **Sutta Pitaka**. The **Second Council** (c. **383 BCE**) at **Vaishali** under **Kalashoka**, led by **Sabbakami**, **addressed corruption in the Sangha and reaffirmed monastic discipline** (traditionally associated with a dispute over the **'Ten Points'** that foreshadowed the later **Sthaviravadin–Mahasanghika** division). The **Third Council** (c. **250 BCE**) at **Pataliputra** under **Ashoka**, presided by **Moggaliputta Tissa**, compiled the **Abhidhamma Pitaka** (the *Kathavatthu*) and dispatched **missionaries** abroad, after which Ashoka raised **84,000 stupas**. The **Fourth Council** (c. **72 CE**) at **Kundalavana in Kashmir** under **Kanishka**, presided by **Vasumitra** with **Ashvaghosha** as deputy, formalised the division into **Mahayana** and **Hinayana** and recorded texts in **Sanskrit**. Together the councils **fixed the Tripitaka** and **institutionalised the schools**, showing how **sustained royal patronage** carried Buddhism from a monastic community to a pan-Asian religion.
keyPoints: 1st (Rajagriha, Ajatashatru, Mahakassapa) — Vinaya & Sutta Pitakas compiled.
2nd (Vaishali, Kalashoka, Sabbakami) — addressed Sangha corruption; reaffirmed monastic discipline ('Ten Points' tradition).
3rd (Pataliputra, Ashoka, Moggaliputta Tissa) — Abhidhamma Pitaka; missionaries; 84,000 stupas.
4th (Kashmir, Kanishka, Vasumitra) — Mahayana–Hinayana split; Sanskrit canon.
Councils fixed the Tripitaka and defined Buddhism's schools under royal patronage.

items.question: Compare the Hinayana, Mahayana and Vajrayana schools of Buddhism. In this context, explain the Bodhisattva ideal and assess the roles of Ashoka and Kanishka in the spread of the faith.
items.modelAnswer: The three schools differ in **conception of the Buddha, goal, and practice**. **Hinayana (Theravada)**, the **'Lesser Path'** or **'Doctrine of the Elders'**, treats the **Buddha as a human teacher**, rejects **idol worship**, and seeks **individual Nirvana** through self-discipline; its **Pali** canon survives in **Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Thailand**, and **Ashoka** was its foremost patron. **Mahayana**, the **'Greater Path'**, deifies the **Buddha**, sanctions **idol and Bodhisattva worship**, uses **mantras**, and aims at the **universal liberation** of all beings; its **Sanskrit** texts spread to **China and Japan** under the patronage of **Kanishka**. **Vajrayana** — the **'Vehicle of the Thunderbolt'** or **Tantric Buddhism** — adds the **Two Truths Doctrine**, **symbolic language** and reverence for the **Guru (Lama)**, flourishing in **Tibet, Nepal and Bhutan**. Central to Mahayana is the **Bodhisattva ideal**: an **enlightened being who postpones personal Nirvana** to help **all beings**, embodying **compassion (karuna)** over solitary release. Politically, **Ashoka** institutionalised Buddhism through the **Third Council**, **edicts** and **missionaries** (including to Sri Lanka), while **Kanishka** championed **Mahayana** at the **Fourth Council**, enabling its **Central Asian and East Asian** diffusion. Thus doctrinal evolution and **royal patronage** together transformed Buddhism into a **world religion**.
keyPoints: Hinayana: human Buddha, no idols, Pali, individual Nirvana; patron Ashoka.
Mahayana: divine Buddha, idol/Bodhisattva worship, Sanskrit, universal liberation; patron Kanishka.
Vajrayana: Tantric, Two Truths, Guru/Lama; Tibet, Nepal, Bhutan.
Bodhisattva ideal: enlightened being deferring Nirvana to save all beings (Mahayana compassion).
Ashoka via 3rd Council/edicts/missionaries; Kanishka via 4th Council spread Mahayana abroad.

items.question: Assess the contribution of Buddhism to Indian art and architecture, with reference to the stupa, chaitya and vihara, the major sculptural schools, and rock-cut cave traditions.
items.modelAnswer: Buddhism was a **prime mover of early Indian art and architecture**. Its signature monument, the **stupa** — a **hemispherical relic shrine** — carried a rich **symbolism**: the **square base** (Earth), **dome/anda** (Water), **harmika** (Fire), **yasti** (Air) and **chattras** (Space), with the spire signifying the **path to enlightenment**. **Ashoka** popularised stupa-building, reputedly raising **84,000** after the Third Council; **Sanchi** and **Bharhut** are the classic examples, later echoed in **dagobas** (Sri Lanka), **chortens** (Tibet) and **pagodas** (East Asia). Congregational worship produced the **chaitya** (prayer hall) and the **vihara** (monastery), best preserved in the **rock-cut caves** of **Ajanta, Ellora and Bhaja**, celebrated for their **murals and sculpture**. Three **sculptural schools** matured under Buddhist patronage: **Gandhara** (Greco-Roman realism), **Mathura** (indigenous images and yakshas) and **Amaravati** (delicate narrative reliefs). The **Sarnath pillar** of Ashoka, crowned by the **Lion Capital**, is today India's **national emblem**. Sustained by **Ashoka, Kanishka, the Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas and Chalukyas**, these forms shaped Indian aesthetics for centuries and endure as **UNESCO World Heritage** sites at **Sanchi, Ajanta, Bodh Gaya and Nalanda**.
keyPoints: Stupa = relic shrine; five elements Earth/Water/Fire/Air/Space (base/dome/harmika/yasti/chattras).
Chaitya (prayer hall) and Vihara (monastery); rock-cut caves at Ajanta, Ellora, Bhaja.
Ashoka's Sarnath Lion Capital = national emblem; 84,000 stupas after the 3rd Council.
Patrons: Ashoka, Kanishka, Satavahanas, Rashtrakutas, Chalukyas; UNESCO sites Sanchi/Ajanta/Bodh Gaya/Nalanda.
